steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper on compressing large vanilla (noise-to-image) GANs such as StyleGAN2 and BigGAN using only the teacher discriminator for distillation. Explain why compressing vanilla GANs is hard, motivate the idea, and list the contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
## Introduction
- GANs are widely used, but the big vanilla GANs are too large to deploy
- Existing GAN compression work, mostly on conditional GANs
- Four difficulties of compressing vanilla GANs
- Our idea: train a narrow generator from scratch, guided by the teacher discriminator
- DGL-GAN and contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
## Introduction
- GANs widely used
  - first proposed in original GAN paper (cite)
  - CV tasks: image generation (cite), image editing (cite), image denoising (cite)
  - noise-to-image: StyleGAN series (cite) and BigGAN (cite) most representative vanilla GANs; diverse photo-realistic images from noise, huge number of params, large high-quality datasets
  - StyleGAN2: 30.37 M params on FFHQ (cite); BigGAN: 70.33 M params on ImageNet (cite)
  - deploying on resource-limited devices urgent + challenging; impedes broader applications
- Existing compression
  - mainstream: reuse image-classification compression techniques: weight pruning, weight quantization, channel pruning, lightweight architecture search/design, evolutionary compression, KD (cite each)
  - most target conditional (cycle) GANs for image-to-image; few on vanilla GANs except recent works (cite)
- Four difficulties
  - (a) pretrained generator sensitive to parameter reduction
    - prune + tune methods (cite) degrade synthesized images; every pixel relates to all channels of kernels/intermediate features (also noted by prior work, cite)
    - mask 1/8 params of kernels in pretrained StyleGAN2 (cite) -> quality intensely affected (Fig. 2)
  - (b) individual input lacks ground truth in noise-to-image
    - ground truth = distribution of real images, not an individual image
    - same latent code z into two independently trained StyleGAN2 generators -> distinct images, similar FID (Fig. 3)
    - aligning student/teacher feature maps may not be feasible; revisit KD in GANs
  - (c) role of pretrained GAN unknown
    - imitating teacher generator features or teacher discriminator logits may not be feasible (Section 4.3); how to use teacher knowledge is mysterious
  - (d) non-convex non-concave minimax structure
    - unstable training (cite); extra challenge for compression
    - teacher discriminator too strong to supervise student generator -> more instability (Section 4.3)
- Our idea
  - train compressed generator from scratch instead of tuning pretrained one (cite); specific KD mechanism expected to alleviate sensitivity
  - (b),(c): transfer info about distribution, not an individual image
  - distribution from teacher generator hard (high-dim images); teacher discriminator implicitly contains it
  - optimal discriminator formulation, Eq. (1) (cite); p_{d} real data distribution, p_{g} synthesized distribution
  - if teacher D near optimal and teacher G better than student (e.g. FID), teacher D may contain better synthesized distribution
  - question: is teacher D more suitable than teacher G for distilling student GANs? answered empirically
  - use only teacher D as extra supervision for student G; two-stage training strategy against minimax instability
- DGL-GAN + contributions
  - Discriminator Guided Learning (DGL-GAN): teacher D only, narrow G from scratch, two-stage training; compress large vanilla GANs, efficient inference
  - teacher D may hold useful info about real/fake distribution; use only adversarial interaction teacher D <-> student G; simple yet effective
  - validated on StyleGAN2 and BigGAN; state-of-the-art for both; StyleGAN2 comparable FID (cite) with 1/3 params on FFHQ; BigGAN comparable IS (cite) with 1/4 params on ImageNet
  - also helps uncompressed StyleGAN2: new state-of-the-art on FFHQ (FID 2.65), surpasses StyleGAN3 (cite)

steps.text:
## Introduction

GANs, which were first proposed in the original GAN paper, have become prevalent for computer vision tasks, for example image generation, image editing, image denoising, and the references therein. For noise-to-image generation, the two most representative vanilla GANs are the StyleGAN series and BigGAN. They can generate diverse photo-realistic images from random noise, but they do this by using a huge number of parameters and large scale high-quality training datasets. Roughly, StyleGAN2 has 30.37 M parameters on Flickr-Faces-HQ (FFHQ), and BigGAN has 70.33 M parameters on ImageNet. Deploying such large GANs on devices with limited computational resources is an urgent and challenging task, and it largely holds back their broader applications.

To make GANs easier to deploy on devices with limited computational resources, a lot of works have been proposed to get lightweight GANs. The main approach is to take the model compression techniques developed for image classification and use them to compress GANs, for example weight pruning, weight quantization, channel pruning, lightweight GAN architecture search/design, evolutionary compression, and knowledge distillation (KD). But most of these works focus on compressing conditional (cycle) GANs for image-to-image generation tasks, and only a few works have been proposed for compressing vanilla GANs, apart from some recent works. Compressing vanilla GANs is difficult mainly for four reasons:

- (a) The existing pretrained generator is sensitive to reducing parameters. Several compression methods prune the pretrained generator and then tune it further. But pruning the pretrained generator will always degrade the quality of the synthesized images, because every pixel in the synthesized image relates to all channels of the convolutional kernels or intermediate features in the generator, as other work has also pointed out. To show this, we mask 1/8 of the parameters of the convolutional kernels in the pretrained StyleGAN2 and generate images with it, shown in Fig. 2, and the quality of the images is intensely affected.

- (b) An individual input does not have a corresponding ground truth in the noise-to-image generation task. We want to stress that the ground truth for a vanilla GAN is a distribution of real images and not an individual image, which means a certain latent code sent to the generator may not have a corresponding ground truth. To show this, we send the same latent code z to two generators of StyleGAN2 that were trained independently and get the synthesized images, shown in Fig. 3. The images are distinct, but the two generators have similar performance, i.e., Fréchet Inception Distance (FID). So since an individual input has no corresponding ground truth, aligning the intermediate or output feature maps of the student generator with the ones of the teacher generator may not be feasible. We need to revisit the KD technique in GANs.

- (c) role of pretrained GAN unknown
  - imitating teacher generator features or teacher discriminator logits may not be feasible (Section 4.3); how to use teacher knowledge is mysterious
- (d) non-convex non-concave minimax structure
  - unstable training (cite); extra challenge for compression
  - teacher discriminator too strong to supervise student generator -> more instability (Section 4.3)
- Our idea
  - train compressed generator from scratch instead of tuning pretrained one (cite)
  - transfer info about distribution, not an individual image; teacher discriminator implicitly contains it
  - optimal discriminator formulation, Eq. (1) (cite); p_{d} real, p_{g} synthesized
  - is teacher D more suitable than teacher G for distilling student GANs? answered empirically
  - only teacher D as extra supervision for student G; two-stage training strategy
- DGL-GAN + contributions
  - Discriminator Guided Learning (DGL-GAN)
  - adversarial interaction teacher D <-> student G only; simple yet effective
  - StyleGAN2 comparable FID (cite) with 1/3 params on FFHQ; BigGAN comparable IS (cite) with 1/4 params on ImageNet
  - uncompressed StyleGAN2: new state-of-the-art on FFHQ (FID 2.65), surpasses StyleGAN3 (cite)

steps.text:
## Introduction

GANs, which were first proposed in the original GAN paper, have become prevalent for computer vision tasks, for example image generation, image editing, image denoising, and the references therein. For noise-to-image generation, the two most representative vanilla GANs are the StyleGAN series and BigGAN. They can generate diverse photo-realistic images from random noise, but they do this by using a huge number of parameters and large scale high-quality training datasets. Roughly, StyleGAN2 has 30.37 M parameters on Flickr-Faces-HQ (FFHQ), and BigGAN has 70.33 M parameters on ImageNet. Deploying such large GANs on devices with limited computational resources is an urgent and challenging task, and it largely holds back their broader applications.

To make GANs easier to deploy on devices with limited computational resources, a lot of works have been proposed to get lightweight GANs. The main approach is to take the model compression techniques developed for image classification and use them to compress GANs, for example weight pruning, weight quantization, channel pruning, lightweight GAN architecture search/design, evolutionary compression, and knowledge distillation (KD). But most of these works focus on compressing conditional (cycle) GANs for image-to-image generation tasks, and only a few works have been proposed for compressing vanilla GANs, apart from some recent works. Compressing vanilla GANs is difficult mainly for four reasons:

- (a) The existing pretrained generator is sensitive to reducing parameters. Several compression methods prune the pretrained generator and then tune it further. But pruning the pretrained generator will always degrade the quality of the synthesized images, because every pixel in the synthesized image relates to all channels of the convolutional kernels or intermediate features in the generator, as other work has also pointed out. To show this, we mask 1/8 of the parameters of the convolutional kernels in the pretrained StyleGAN2 and generate images with it, shown in Fig. 2, and the quality of the images is intensely affected.

- (b) An individual input does not have a corresponding ground truth in the noise-to-image generation task. We want to stress that the ground truth for a vanilla GAN is a distribution of real images and not an individual image, which means a certain latent code sent to the generator may not have a corresponding ground truth. To show this, we send the same latent code z to two generators of StyleGAN2 that were trained independently and get the synthesized images, shown in Fig. 3. The images are distinct, but the two generators have similar performance, i.e., Fréchet Inception Distance (FID). So since an individual input has no corresponding ground truth, aligning the intermediate or output feature maps of the student generator with the ones of the teacher generator may not be feasible. We need to revisit the KD technique in GANs.

- (c) The role of a pretrained GAN model in compressing vanilla GANs is unknown. Following from the point above, there is no ground truth for an individual input, which means directly imitating the teacher generator in the feature space, or the logits of the teacher discriminator, may not be feasible, which our experiments in Section 4.3 verify. How to effectively use the knowledge of teacher GANs is mysterious.

- (d) The non-convex non-concave minimax structure of GAN makes compression harder. The non-convex non-concave minimax structure makes GAN training unstable, which is an additional challenge for compression. Directly bringing in teacher GANs, especially the teacher discriminator, could make training the student GANs even more unstable, because the pretrained teacher discriminator is too strong to give appropriate supervision to the student generator, which we also show with experiments in Section 4.3.

Because the pretrained generator is sensitive to reducing parameters, we train a compressed generator directly from scratch instead of tuning from the pretrained generator like previous methods. We expect that training a compressed generator directly with the specific knowledge distillation mechanism we introduce will alleviate the sensitivity to parameters. Considering difficulty (b) and difficulty (c), what we want to bring in from the teacher GAN is information about the distribution, not an individual synthesized image. Getting the distribution directly from the teacher generator is highly non-trivial, because images are high-dimensional. But the teacher discriminator implicitly contains information about the distribution. Recall the optimal formulation of the discriminator from the original GAN paper, Eq. (1), where p_{d} is the distribution of the real datasets and p_{g} is the distribution of the synthesized images. Suppose the teacher discriminator reaches or approaches the optimal formulation in Eq. (1) and the teacher generator performs better than the student generator (in terms of certain divergence metrics, e.g., FID). Then compared with the student discriminator, the teacher discriminator may contain a better synthesized distribution. So a natural question comes up: is the teacher discriminator more suitable for distilling student GANs than the teacher generator? In this work we answer this question from empirical perspectives. Specifically, we propose to use only the teacher discriminator as the additional source of supervision signal for the student generator. Also, to reduce the instability caused by the minimax objective function, we propose a two-stage training strategy to stabilize the optimization process.

In short, our framework only uses the teacher discriminator and trains a narrow generator from scratch, with a two-stage training strategy to stabilize the optimization process. We call it the Discriminator Guided Learning approach, abbreviated as DGL-GAN, and it aims at compressing large-scale vanilla GANs and making inference efficient. Our contributions are:

- • Motivated by the intuition that the teacher discriminator may contain some useful information about the distribution of real images and fake images, we only use the adversarial interaction between the teacher discriminator and the student generator to help the student generator, which is simple yet effective.

- • We validate DGL-GAN on two representative large-scale vanilla GANs, StyleGAN2 and BigGAN. DGL-GAN achieves state-of-the-art for compressing both StyleGAN2 and BigGAN. With DGL-GAN, the compressed StyleGAN2 gets comparable Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) using only 1/3 of the parameters on FFHQ, and the compressed BigGAN gets comparable Inception Score (IS) using only 1/4 of the parameters on ImageNet.

- • DGL-GAN is not limited to compressed vanilla GANs, it also improves the performance of the original uncompressed StyleGAN2, and achieves a new state-of-the-art performance on FFHQ (FID 2.65), even better than StyleGAN3.

For noise-to-image generation, the two most representative vanilla GANs are the StyleGAN series [2,3,15] and BigGAN [4]. They can generate diverse photo-realistic images from random noise, but they do this by using a huge number of parameters and large scale high-quality training datasets. To make GANs easier to deploy on devices with limited computational resources, a lot of works have been proposed to get lightweight GANs. The main approach is to take the model compression techniques developed for image classification and use them to compress GANs, for example weight pruning [17], weight quantization [18], channel pruning [19,20,21,22], lightweight GAN architecture search/design [23,24,25,26], evolutionary compression [27,28], and knowledge distillation (KD) [29,30,31,32,33,34,35,36]. But most of these works focus on compressing conditional (cycle) GANs for image-to-image generation tasks, and only a few works have been proposed for compressing vanilla GANs, apart from some recent works [20,21,30,11,37,38]. Compressing vanilla GANs is difficult mainly for four reasons:

- (a) The existing pretrained generator is sensitive to reducing parameters. Several compression methods [20,11] prune the pretrained generator and then tune it further. But pruning the pretrained generator will always degrade the quality of the synthesized images, because every pixel in the synthesized image relates to all channels of the convolutional kernels or intermediate features in the generator, as other work has also pointed out [30]. - (b) An individual input does not have a corresponding ground truth in the noise-to-image generation task. How to effectively use the knowledge of teacher GANs is mysterious.

- (d) The non-convex non-concave minimax structure of GAN makes compression harder. The non-convex non-concave minimax structure makes GAN training unstable [39,40], which is an additional challenge for compression. Directly bringing in teacher GANs, especially the teacher discriminator, could make training the student GANs even more unstable, because the pretrained teacher discriminator is too strong to give appropriate supervision to the student generator, which we also show with experiments in Section 4.3.

Because the pretrained generator is sensitive to reducing parameters, we train a compressed generator directly from scratch instead of tuning from the pretrained generator like previous methods [20,11]. We expect that training a compressed generator directly with the specific knowledge distillation mechanism we introduce will alleviate the sensitivity to parameters. Considering difficulty (b) and difficulty (c), what we want to bring in from the teacher GAN is information about the distribution, not an individual synthesized image. Getting the distribution directly from the teacher generator is highly non-trivial, because images are high-dimensional. But the teacher discriminator implicitly contains information about the distribution. Recall the optimal formulation of the discriminator from the original GAN paper [1], Eq. (1), where p_{d} is the distribution of the real datasets and p_{g} is the distribution of the synthesized images. steps.text:
## Introduction

GANs, first proposed in [1], have been prevalent for computer vision tasks, see, e.g., image generation [2,3,4,5,6,7], image editing [8,9,10,11,12], image denoising [13,14], and the references therein. For noise-to-image generation, two of the most representative vanilla GANs are the StyleGAN series [2,3,15] and BigGAN [4], which can generate diverse photo-realistic images from random noise by using a huge number of parameters and large scale high-quality training datasets. Roughly speaking, StyleGAN2 contains 30.37 M parameters on Flickr-Faces-HQ (FFHQ) [2], and BigGAN contains 70.33 M parameters on ImageNet [16]. Deploying such large-scale GANs on computational resource-limited devices is an urgent and challenging task, and this largely impedes their broader applications.

To make GANs easy to deploy on computational resource limited devices, extensive works have been proposed to obtain lightweight GANs. The mainstream approach is to inherit the model compression techniques developed for image classification to compress GANs, such as weight pruning [17], weight quantization [18], channel pruning [19,20,21,22], lightweight GAN architecture search/design [23,24,25,26], evolutionary compression [27,28], and knowledge distillation (KD) [29,30,31,32,33,34,35,36]. However, most of the above works focus on compressing conditional (cycle) GANs for image-to-image generation tasks, and scarce works have been proposed for compressing vanilla GANs, except recent works [20,21,30,11,37,38]. The difficulties of compressing vanilla GANs mainly lie in four aspects:

- (a) The existing pretrained generator is sensitive to the reduction of parameters. Several compression methods [20,11] conduct pruning on the pretrained generator and further tune it. However, pruning the pretrained generator will inevitably degrade the quality of synthesized images, because every pixel in the synthesized image relates to all channels of the convolutional kernels or intermediate features in the generator, as also pointed out in [30]. To illustrate this, we mask 1/8 of the parameters of the convolutional kernels in the pretrained StyleGAN2 [3] and generate images with it, presented in Fig. 2, where the quality of the images is intensely affected.

- (b) An individual input lacks the corresponding ground truth in the noise-to-image generation task. What we want to emphasize is that the ground truth for a vanilla GAN is a distribution of real images rather than an individual image, which means that a certain latent code sent to the generator may not have a corresponding ground truth. To illustrate this, we send the same latent code z to two independently trained generators of StyleGAN2 and obtain the synthesized images, shown in Fig. 3. The images are distinct, yet the two generators have similar performance, i.e., Fréchet Inception Distance (FID). Thus, given that an individual input lacks the corresponding ground truth, aligning the intermediate or output feature maps of the student generator with those of the teacher generator may not be feasible. We need to revisit the KD technique in GANs.

- (c) The role of a pretrained GAN model in compressing vanilla GANs is unknown. Given the above point, ground truth is absent for an individual input, which means that directly imitating the teacher generator in the feature space or the logits of the teacher discriminator may not be feasible, as verified by our experiments in Section 4.3. How to effectively leverage the knowledge of teacher GANs remains mysterious.

- (d) The non-convex non-concave minimax structure of GAN increases the difficulty of compression. The non-convex non-concave minimax structure causes unstable training of GANs [39,40], imposing an additional challenge on compression. Directly introducing teacher GANs, especially the teacher discriminator, could aggravate the instability of training student GANs, since the pretrained teacher discriminator is too strong to provide appropriate supervision for the student generator, as also demonstrated via experiments in Section 4.3.

Given the sensitivity of the pretrained generator to the reduction of parameters, we directly train a compressed generator from scratch, rather than tuning from the pretrained generator [20,11]. We expect that directly training a compressed generator with the specific knowledge distillation mechanism we introduce will alleviate the sensitivity to parameters. Taking difficulties (b) and (c) into account, what we want to introduce from the teacher GAN is information about the distribution rather than an individual synthesized image. Directly obtaining the distribution from the teacher generator is highly non-trivial due to the high dimension of images. However, the teacher discriminator implicitly contains information about the distribution. Recall the optimal formulation of the discriminator in [1], Eq. (1), where p_{d} is the distribution of the real datasets and p_{g} is the distribution of synthesized images. Supposing that the teacher discriminator reaches or approaches the optimal formulation in Eq. (1) and the teacher generator achieves superior performance to the student generator (regarding certain divergence metrics, e.g., FID), the teacher discriminator may contain a better synthesized distribution than the student discriminator. A natural question arises: is the teacher discriminator more suitable for distilling student GANs than the teacher generator? In this work, we answer this question from empirical perspectives. Specifically, we propose to exploit only the teacher discriminator as the additional source of the supervision signal for the student generator. Moreover, to alleviate the instability caused by the minimax objective function, we propose a two-stage training strategy to stabilize the optimization process.

In a word, our framework only utilizes the teacher discriminator and trains a narrow generator from scratch, with a two-stage training strategy to stabilize the optimization process. We denote it the Discriminator Guided Learning approach, abbreviated as DGL-GAN, aiming at compressing large-scale vanilla GANs and making inference efficient. Our contributions can be summarized as follows:

- • Motivated by the intuition that the teacher discriminator may contain some useful information about the distribution of real images and fake images, we merely exploit the adversarial interaction between the teacher discriminator and the student generator to facilitate the student generator, which is simple yet effective.

- • We validate DGL-GAN on two representative large-scale vanilla GANs, StyleGAN2 and BigGAN. DGL-GAN achieves state-of-the-art in compressing both StyleGAN2 and BigGAN. With DGL-GAN, the compressed StyleGAN2 achieves comparable Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) [41] using only 1/3 of the parameters on FFHQ, and the compressed BigGAN achieves comparable Inception Score (IS) [39] using only 1/4 of the parameters on ImageNet.

- • Not confined to compressed vanilla GANs, DGL-GAN also improves the performance of the original uncompressed StyleGAN2, achieving a new state-of-the-art performance on FFHQ (FID 2.65), even surpassing StyleGAN3 [15].
